name: Scotch Ale (Wee Heavy)
title: Scotch Ale and Wee Heavy: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Scotch ale, or wee heavy: a strong, malty Scottish ale full of caramel. How it tastes, how to serve it and what Indian food to pair.
tagline: Strong, malty and warming. The Scottish answer to cold weather, best taken slowly.
tastes:
Wee heavy is the strong end of the Scottish brewing tradition. The name comes from small bottles of heavy, strong ale. Scotland's cool climate and hop shortage pushed its brewers towards malt-led beers, and this style is that idea taken all the way.

In the glass it is about malt. Caramel and toffee first, then dark fruit, bread crust and sometimes a light nuttiness. Long kettle boils caramelise some of the wort, which deepens the colour and the flavour. Hop bitterness is low, just enough to stop it being syrupy. Alcohol, usually 6 to 8 percent and sometimes more, shows as a gentle warmth.

A common myth: Scotch ales should taste of peat smoke. Traditional Scottish ale malt was not peated, and a strong peat note is usually a brewer reaching for whisky imagery. A faint earthy note is fine. A beer that smells like a bonfire is a different style. The clean, cool fermentation keeps the focus on malt sweetness and body.

profile.look: Deep copper to dark brown, often with ruby highlights. Clear. Creamy, light tan head that may fade fast at higher strengths.
profile.aroma_flavour: Caramel, toffee, raisin and toasted bread. Low hop character. Clean, with few esters. Alcohol shows as warmth. Peat smoke, if present at all, should be faint.
profile.mouthfeel: Full, chewy body with low to moderate carbonation. A sweet, warming finish that stays smooth.
profile.ingredients: Scottish or English pale malt, a little crystal and a touch of roasted barley for colour. Sometimes a long boil for kettle caramelisation. Sparing English hops. Clean, cool-fermenting ale yeast.

in_india: Whisky has made Scotland a familiar idea to Indian drinkers, and a wee heavy is an easy bridge for someone who usually orders a peg. It is a slow, cool-weather beer: Delhi in January, Bengaluru in December, a Diwali party where the food runs late. Its strength and low hops mean it keeps reasonably well, but heat still dulls it towards dried fruit and sherry. Several Indian brewpubs and at least one large craft brand have brewed one, often for the winter festive season.

pairings.why: The beer's malt sweetness cools the Mathania chilli, and its body matches the rich mutton gravy.
Butter, cream and tomato love caramel malt, and the warmth of the beer stands up to the gravy.

pairings.food: Aged cheddar with fig or date chutney
pairings.why: Sharp cheese against toffee malt is a classic, and the fruit chutney picks up the raisin notes.
Cashew and sugar meet toffee and bread crust, and the alcohol keeps the sweetness from piling up.
